I stopped giving stars about four years ago and my editor has never quite forgiven me. The argument for stars is that readers are busy, which is true. The argument against them is that a star rating is a verdict with the reasons removed, and the reasons are the only part of my job that has any value. If I tell you a production is uneven, you have learned almost nothing. If I tell you that the first act is twenty minutes too long and that the second is the best thing the company has done in a decade, you can decide for yourself whether that trade is worth your Saturday. The other thing I have learned, slowly and against my instincts, is that I should not review anything on the opening night. The room is full of people who are not there to watch a play. They are there to be seen having watched it, and that changes what happens on stage more than anybody admits.

I saw the same play twice, ten years apart, with two different casts, and I have thought about it ever since, because I did not change my mind about the production. I changed my mind about the ending. The first time I was thirty and I thought the ending was sentimental and unearned, and I remember being quite pleased with myself for noticing. The second time I was forty and the same ending completely destroyed me. Nothing in the staging was different. What was different is that I had been through the thing the play is about, and at thirty I simply had not. I am not sure what that says about criticism, honestly. Maybe only that a review is a record of what one person could see on one evening, which is worth reading and is not the same thing as a measurement.
